newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan considers selling surplus soymeal to China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan considers selling surplus soymeal to China.

text.p: Taiwan edible oil producers said on Monday they were considering exporting soymeal to China as the island's pork export crisis sent soybean inventories soaring and local prices falling.
"The massive slaughter of pigs will significantly reduce demand for soymeal," Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Co official Jack Lee told Reuters.
Lee said soymeal producers were considering exporting soymeal to other Asian importers, including China.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has projected China's 1996/97 soymeal imports at 1.3 million tonnes, up from 1.1 million in 1995/96 and near zero prior to that.
China, once a significant exporter, now imports soymeal to cover soaring consumption for animal feed.
Taiwan soymeal was quoted at around US$360 per tonne on a cost and freight basis on Monday, higher than the U.S. low-protein soymeal price of US$356, traders said.
Taiwan's soymeal protein level is about 43 percent.
Traders said local soymeal prices were likely to fall further as Taiwan's battle with hog foot and mouth disease continues.
In 1996, Taiwan imported about 2.4 million tonnes of soybeans, which could produce up to 1.9 million tonnes of soymeal after crushing, traders said.
Taiwan on Monday ordered hog trading halted for three days at 19 of the island's 22 major hog wholesale centres as troops began slaughtering all pigs at infected farms.
"We are conducting a massive slaughter in 19 counties and trading must be halted to stop movements of pigs," an official of the cabinet's Council of Agriculture said.
Local pork prices have plunged by as much as 60 percent since Thursday, when the council reported the epidemic and banned all fresh and frozen pork exports.
The council estimated six million of the 14 million hogs raised each year in Taiwan were exported.

Farm experts backed by germ-suited soldiers late on Friday began the process of slaughtering an estimated 100,000 or more hogs at farms stricken with the fatal disease, which is highly contagious and can spread through the air.
According to a council survey in 1994, the hog industry's net value stood at T$89 billion, comprising 20 percent of Taiwan's farm production value and 60 percent of the livestock value.
Taiwan's pork exports ban could lead to a 10 percent fall in soybean imports.
"We don't see much demand for soymeal now, so we must reduce our soybean imports," Taiwan Formosa Oilseed manager Steven Kuo said.
